abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Although the COVID-19 pandemic has officially ended, outbreaks still occur, especially in immunocompromised patients, including those undergoing chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy, who have weakened immune systems due to prior treatments or CAR T-related effects such as severe and prolonged neutropenia, lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia. This retrospective study analyzed relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy, assessing the impact of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection on overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and delays in leukapheresis and CAR T-cell infusion. Among 89 infused patients, 37 (41.6%) developed COVID-19. Compared to the COVID + cohort, COVID- patients had worse prognostic scores and higher LDH and ferritin levels before infusion. SARS-CoV-2 infection delayed leukapheresis (14–35 days) and CAR T-cell infusion (20–65 days). The best overall response rate (BRR) in the CAR T-cell population was 77.5% (69/89 patients), with a complete response (CR) rate of 67%. The BRR was 100% in COVID + patients vs. 61.5% in COVID−. Median PFS was 5.47 months in the COVID- cohort and not reached in the COVID + cohort (p = 0.007). Median OS was 19 months in COVID- patients and not reached in COVID+ (p < 0.0001). No significant survival differences were found between COVID + and COVID − patients. Improved outcomes likely resulted from widespread vaccination, prophylaxis, early antiviral treatments, and the emergence of less virulent SARS-CoV-2 variants, reducing disease severity and mortality, allowing for better management of these patients.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Patients with hematological malignancies are vulnerable patients at increased risk of infection due to both patient (e.g. comorbidities, age, ethnicity, compliance with prophylaxis and vaccination) and disease characteristics with related medical history (e.g. the lymphoma itself, previous immuno-chemotherapies or stem-cell transplantation) [1, 2]. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy has proven to be an effective strategy for patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (R/R LBCL) [3, 4]. However, CAR T-cell therapy is often associated with adverse events (AEs), the most common of which are cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurological toxicity (immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome [ICANS]) [5]. Of note, also the risk of infection in these patients is not irrelevant due to additional factors like lymphodepletion (LD) induced neutropenia and T-cell suppression/immunodeficiency, B-cell aplasia/hypogammaglobulinemia and the type, dose and duration of drugs used to manage major AEs, such as tocilizumab, steroids and a broad spectrum antibiotics [6].

On December 31st 2019, only a few months after the approval by Italian Medicines Agency (AIFA) of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) for the treatment of LBCL R/R to two or more prior lines of therapy, the Wuhan Municipal Health Commission (China) reported a first cluster of pneumonia cases caused by a new coronavirus, called Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Corona Virus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) [7]. On March 11, 2020, due to the rapid spread of COVID-19 disease, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a pandemic status [8]. In Italy, epidemiological monitoring by the Istituto Superiore di Sanità (ISS) recorded alternating waves of incidence and the evolution of genetic mutations of SARS-CoV-2 during its transmission, recording the occurrence of more aggressive variants, defined SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern (VOCs) with increased pathogenicity and infectivity, with multiple sub-variants and sub-branches [9]. The main variants were B.1.1.7 (“English” or Alpha), B.1.0351 (“South African” or Beta), P.1 (“Brazilian” or Gamma), B.1.617.2 (“Indian” or Delta) and B.1.1.529 (Omicron) [10]. The first wave occurred between February and June 2020. Due to a rapid spread of the disease with an increased mortality, from the 9 March 2020 the Italian government declared a national lockdown, which led to a reduction in the number of infections. However, a new and gradual increase in COVID-19 cases during the summer 2020, led to a second wave between October 2020 and July 2021.

As of December 2020, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved the first vaccines for the prevention of COVID-19: two were mRNA vaccines (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273) composed of modified-nucleoside mRNA encoding for a spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, while the other one (ChAdOx1-S) was a viral vector vaccine [11, 12].

In Italy, the vaccination campaign began on 27 December 2020, starting with people considered frail due to age or comorbidities, such as hematological patients on immunosuppressive or myelosuppressive therapies or patients who have completed treatments for the underlying disease in the previous six months [13]. Between December 2020 and March 2022, 85.5% of the Italian population received at least one dose, 80.2% completed the initial vaccine protocol, and 63.5% received a booster dose [10].

Despite the protection provided by the vaccines, a third wave of infections will occur between July and September 2021, mainly due to the Delta variant, which was found to be the dominant and most transmissible variant [10]; this will be followed by a fourth wave of infections between October 2021 and February 2022, 80% of which will be due to Omicron, according to the ISS surveillance report of 3 January 2022, while only 6% will be due to Delta variant [14].

Although as of 5 May 2023, the WHO has declared that SARS-CoV-2 infection was no longer a public health emergency, it remains an important risk for immunocompromised patients including those with hematological malignancies, who are still at risk of developing severe and potentially fatal forms of COVID-19 [15]. Indeed, recent studies have reported a COVID-19-related mortality of 29–42% in patients with hematological diseases, compared with 2–7% in the general population [16]. To date, in Italy SARS-CoV-2 positive cases are still being reported, thus the management of this infection in immunocompromised patients is still a current clinical practice.

Unfortunately, there is still a lack of studies of COVID-19 in patients receiving cellular therapies, including CAR T-cell, who may have an impaired immune system due to severe and prolonged neutropenia, lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia induced either by previous treatments or by CAR T-cell itself or the management of the immunotherapy-related AEs. In fact, only a small number of case reports or case series have been reported in literature [17, 18, 19].

Here, we report the experience of a large Italian hub center with COVID-19 infections in adult patients with R/R LBCL candidate to CAR T-cell program, from leukapheresis, to test the potential impact of infection in this particular setting of patients, both in terms of treatment pathway and clinical outcome as SARS-CoV-2 is still circulating.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: We conducted a retrospective, monocentric study to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of CAR T-cell therapy in patients with R/R LBCL treated with axi-cel or tisa-cel, according to clinical practice, from August 2019 to November 2023.

Patients were eligible if they were at least 18 years of age, had histologically confirmed LBCL and had been treated with CAR T-cell as per clinical practice (patients treated within a clinical trial context were excluded). All patients provided written informed consent (where applicable). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional committee (AVEC Ethics Committee of Bologna, approval ID 1043/2021/Oss/AOUBo).

Patient and disease information were collected, including demographics, clinical and biological data (e.g. CAR-HEMATOTOX score), prior therapies received, CAR T-cell indications, outcome and associated toxicities. We also analyzed data on bridging therapy (BT), and on disease status prior to CAR T-cell infusion.

Regarding SARS-CoV-2 infection, we collected information on vaccination status (number of doses performed, both pre and post CAR T-cell infusion), number and severity of infections before and after CAR T-cell therapy (e.g. occurred one month before leukapheresis, following the last line of pre-CAR T-cell therapy; after leukapheresis and before CAR T-cell infusion, and after CAR T-cell infusion until subsequent lymphoma therapy or the last available follow-up whichever came first), antiviral therapies used, need for hospitalization and COVID-related deaths. Infected patients were treated as per medical decision and as needed, with the anti-COVID drugs approved and available in Italy at the time of infection, i.e. during the various phase of the pandemic.

As we are a hub center, right after AIFA accreditation (2019) we conceived and created a specific database dedicated to CAR T patients and no missing data are present in the clinical and treatment section starting from the first visit (referral). The section dedicated to COVID infection however - and obviously - was implemented after the declaration of the pandemic status. Thus, rather than having missing data within the individual variables, we have two missing variables: type of vaccines and variants of infections who were not retrievable in patients chart.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Specifically, the aim of our study was to retrospectively investigate the impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the survival of patients with R/R LBCL treated with CAR T-cell therapy.

The primary endpoint was to evaluate the overall survival (OS), both in the COVID + cohort vs. the COVID- cohort, which represents the period between the CAR T-cell infusion and the time of the patient’s death from any cause [20]; in the case of patients who were still alive at data cut-off, the date of the last available follow-up was used.

The secondary endpoints were (1) the progression-free survival (PFS), both in the COVID + cohort vs. the COVID- cohort, which represents the period between the CAR T-cell infusion and the time of the patient’s disease progression, relapse or death from any cause [20]; in the case of patients who were still alive at data cut-off, the date of the last available follow-up was used; (2) to assess whether COVID-19 resulted in delays during treatment in terms of delays in leukapheresis or infusion of the CAR T-cell product.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Demographic data and patient characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Comparison between groups was performed for categorical variables using contingency table analysis with chi-squared or Fisher’s test, as appropriate, while continuous data were analyzed using Student’s t-test after checking that the data were normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk). Comparison of survival between subgroups was performed using Kaplan-Meier product-limit survival curve estimates and log rank tests. Univariate and multivariate analyses were also conducted to investigate which variables could influence patients outcomes. All tests were two-tailed, and a P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 (StataCorp LP, TX).

sec.title: Procedures associated with CAR T-cell therapy
sec.p: All patients underwent lymphocyte-apheresis followed by CAR T-cell infusion. Bridging therapy (BT) was given per the treating physician’s discretion to control or debulk disease prior to CAR T-cell infusion. Prior to infusion, all patients received conditioning chemotherapy consisting of intravenous fludarabine and cyclophosphamide from day − 5 to day − 3. The dosage of this regimen varied according to the infused product, specifically prior to infusion of axi-cel, fludarabine (30 mg/m² body-surface area per day) and cyclophosphamide (500 mg/m² body-surface area per day) were administered, while prior to infusion of tisa-cel, fludarabine 25 mg/m2 and cyclophosphamide 250 mg/m2.

sec.title: SARS-CoV-2 vaccination program, antimicrobial prophylaxis and infections
sec.p: According to the period of vaccines availability and patients’ willingness, patients were vaccinated both before and 3 months after CAR T-cell infusion, with the number of doses varying from one to four. Following CAR T-cell therapy, all patients received antimicrobial prophylaxis starting on the day the neutrophil count was below 1000/ mm3, as per guidelines. Patients without colonizing bacterial isolates received prophylactic antibiotic therapy with levofloxacin. For antifungal prophylaxis, patients were treated with Posaconazole [21].

Acyclovir was also started from the day of infusion. Therapy to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJP) pneumonia, mostly with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, was already ongoing at the time of infusion, as prophylactic therapy provided from previous treatments. Acyclovir and PJP prophylaxis were given for up to 12 months after CAR T-cell therapy or until the CD4 + lymphocyte count was above 200 cells/mm3, as per guidelines [21].

Confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 were defined by positive reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction testing of nasopharyngeal swab specimens. COVID-19 infections that occurred 30 days before apheresis but after the last line of pre-CART therapy, those that occurred in the time between leukapheresis and infusion, and those that occurred after CAR T-cell infusion but before any subsequent lymphoma therapy were analyzed. In these patients, we also evaluated the time between the SARS-CoV-2 infection and the CAR T-cell infusion, the duration of the positive swab, the severity of the infection and whether antiviral therapy or hospitalization was required.

Infection severity was graded according to National Institute of Health (NIH) criteria as follows: (1) asymptomatic or paucisymptomatic those who resolved with few associated symptoms such as cold syndrome, cough, or sore throat and did not require therapy; (2) mild those without dyspnea/abnormal chest imaging requiring oral or intravenous therapy in a day hospital setting; (3) moderate those with clinical/imaging evidence of lower respiratory tract disease and SpO2 ≥ 94% on air requiring hospitalization; (4) severe those with SpO2 < 94% on air; respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min; >50% lung infiltrates, requiring hospitalization and associated with life-threatening symptoms; and (5) critical those with respiratory failure, septic shock, and/or multiple organ dysfunction.

sec.title: Patients characteristics
sec.p: Between August 2019 and November 2023, 89 patients with LBCL relapsed after or refractory to at least two previous lines of therapy, including an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and anthracycline based regimen, received CAR T-cell therapy (64 axi-cel, 25 tisa-cel) at our Institution.

Within this population, 37 (41.5%) patients developed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID + cohort), and 52 (58.4%) patients did not (COVID- cohort). Clinical and demographic characteristics for the whole study sample and separately for the two cohorts, are shown in Table 1.

sec.p: Seventy of the 89 (78.6%) infused patients, of which 29 belonged to the COVID + cohort, received at least one course of BT (including chemo-immunotherapy, steroids, drug conjugated antibodies, checkpoint inhibitors, and radiotherapy). BT resulted in disease control in 17% (5/29) of COVID + patients (1 complete response [CR] and 4 partial responses [PR]), and in 27% (11/41) of patients in the COVID- cohort (3 CR and 8 PR). The median time between apheresis and infusion was 46 days in the COVID + cohort (28–385) and 47 days in the COVID- cohort (38–427).
According to CAR-HEMATOTOX score, five patients (13.5%) in the COVID + cohort and 15 (28.9%) in the COVID- cohort were at high risk of developing a late-onset neutropenia (p 0.1226).

Looking at the main laboratory variables that indicate a disease with a high tumor burden: we have seen that a statistically significant proportion of patients with pre-lymphodepletion (LD) elevated LDH levels (> 250 IU/L) was observed in the COVID- cohort compared to the COVID + cohort (44.2% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.0025), as well as pre-LD ferritin, which was higher in the COVID- cohort (21.2% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.0025), while no statistically significant difference in CRP levels was seen between the two cohorts (40.4% vs. 35.1%, p = 0.6629). A minority of patients had severe hypogammaglobulinemia prior to CAR T-cell infusion (COVID- 28.9% vs. COVID + 16.2%, p = 0.2097) (Table 1).

Prior to being candidates for CART, fifteen patients were unvaccinated (16.9%), while 54 (60.7%) received a median of 3 doses (1–5) of one of the available vaccines against SARS-CoV-2. Post CAR T-cell infusion, all fifteen patients were vaccinated, for a total of twenty-seven vaccinated patients (30.3%), with a median number of doses of 2 (1–4). All characteristics regarding the number of doses of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine received both before and after CAR T-cell are shown in Table 2. Twenty-one patients (23.6%) also received prophylactic tixagevimab-cilgavimab, including 4 patients who received it prior to infusion (19%) and 17 patients received it post-infusion (81%).

sec.title: SARS-CoV-2 infection characteristics
sec.p: Of the thirty-seven patients in the COVID + cohort, eight (21.6%) contracted SARS-CoV-2 infection before CAR T-cell infusion, twenty-six (70.3%) after CAR T-cell infusion and three patients (8.1%) had infection both before and after.

In particular, seven patients with infection before CAR T-cell also had it before leukapheresis and one patient after leukapheresis during BT. In addition, of the three patients who had the infection both before and after the CAR T-cell infusion, two had it before leukapheresis and one had it between leukapheresis and infusion during BT.

Due to SARS-CoV-2 infection, 2 patients (2.2%) delayed their scheduled leukapheresis by 14 days and 35 days, and 2 patients delayed their scheduled CAR T-cell infusion by 20 days and 65 days from the date of admission for CAR T-cell infusion.

Eleven patients (29.7%) developed multiple SARS-CoV-2 infections, ranging from 2 to 4 events, for a total of 50 events (Table 2). Of these, twelve events (31.6%) occurred within six months after infusion, 8 (21%) occurred between 6 and 12 months and 18 (47.4%) occurred after 12 months, including 4 (10.5%) after 24 months from CAR T-cell infusion, as shown in Fig. 1. For patients in whom SARS-CoV-2 infections occurred after infusion, the median time from CAR T-cell infusion to diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection was 344 days (5-912), corresponding to 11.3 months.

caption.p: Time from diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection to CAR T-cell infusion

sec.p: Overall, the median time of the duration of SARS-CoV-2 swab positivity was 15 days: in 16 cases between 7 and 13 days (32%), while in 20 infectious events (52.3%) persistent swab positivity was found beyond 21 days (long COVID).

Thirteen patients underwent CAR T-cell infusion before vaccines became available in Italy; among them, eight were vaccinated after receiving the CAR-T product. Prior to being considered for CAR T-cell therapy, 15 patients (16.9%) were unvaccinated, while 54 patients (60.7%) had received a median of 3 vaccine doses (range 1–5) against SARS-CoV-2. Following CAR T-cell infusion, all 15 previously unvaccinated patients were subsequently vaccinated, bringing the total number of post-infusion vaccinated patients to 27 (30.3%), with a median of 2 doses (range 1–4).

Thirty-seven COVID-19 infectious events were classified as at least moderate, requiring oral or intravenous antiviral therapy. Of these, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was used in twenty-one SARS-CoV-2 infections (56.7%), remdesvir in 12 (32.4%), monoclonal antibodies (sotrovimab, casirivimab-imdevimab) in 7 (18.9%) and an off-label combination of remdesivir and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in 3 (8.1%) cases. In addition, a therapeutic dose of tixagevimab-cilgavimab was administered in 4 cases (10.8%), as shown in Fig. 2. Hospitalization was necessary in 30% of infectious events (15/50), with a median duration of 12 days (2–42).

caption.p: Antiviral therapies used to treat COVID-19 infectious

sec.p: We also examined how our patients were treated across different phases of the COVID-19 pandemic and their outcomes (Supplementary Table 1). Notably, three patients received CAR T-cell infusions in 2019 and did not contract SARS-CoV-2. In 2020, ten patients underwent CAR T-cell therapy, five of whom developed infections during or after the fourth wave. In 2021, twenty-six patients received the infusion, with eleven subsequently developing infections. Unfortunately, data regarding the specific SARS-CoV-2 variants involved and type if vaccines involved were not available.

Among the 37 COVID + patients, 35 (94.6%) cleared their SARS-CoV-2 infection after a median of 15 days (range: 2–413), while the mortality rate due to SARS-CoV-2 infection following CAR T-cell therapy was 5.4%. Of the 89 infused patients, four died from COVID-19, including two in the COVID + cohort and two in the COVID − cohort, who were receiving lymphoma treatment after CAR T-cell infusion. Specifically, 2 patients died in 2020, when the wild-type variant was dominant, one died in 2021, when the Alpha and Delta variants emerged, and the last one died in 2022, when Omicron became the dominant variant.

sec.title: Efficacy, safety and survival
sec.p: At a median follow-up of 20 months, no statistically significant difference between the COVID + and COVID- cohorts were registered in terms of survivals and safety.

In terms of best overall response rate (BRR) for all patients infused, we observed a BRR of 77.5% (69/89 patients), with 67% CR in the CAR T-cell population. The BRR was 100% in the COVID + cohort and 61.5% (32/52 patients) in the COVID- cohort.

Considering all patients infused (n = 89), the mPFS was 16.5 months (Fig. 3a). Twenty-eight patients (31. 5%) died: 4 in the COVID + cohort (2 due to COVID-19 and 2 due to PD) and 24 in the COVID- cohort (18 due to PD, 2 due to ICANS grade 5, 1 due to septic shock, and 1 due to myocardial infarction. Additionally, 2 patients died from COVID-19 contracted during lymphoma therapy following CAR T-cell treatment). The mPFS for the COVID- cohort was 5.47 months, while it was not reached for the COVID + cohort; this difference was statistically significant. At 45 months, PFS was 60% in the COVID + cohort compared to 32% in the COVID- cohort (Fig. 3c). PFS in the group of patients who had SARS-CoV-2 infection only before leukapheresis or after CAR T-cell infusion was also analyzed, but no statistically significant differences were observed.

caption.p: a b Progression free survival (PFS) and Overall survival (OS) in the CAR-T population, calculated from the CAR-T cells infusion. c d: PFS and OS in the COVID + versus COVID- cohorts

sec.p: The median OS of the whole population was not reached (Fig. 3b). The mOS of the COVID- cohort was 19 months, while it was not reached for the COVID + cohort. This difference was also statistically significant (p < 0.0001) as shown in Fig. 3d.

Regarding toxicities, after CAR T-cell infusion, seventy-seven out of 89 patients (86.5%) developed any grade of CRS, of which 5.2% were grade 3 or higher. Twenty-two developed any grade of ICANS (24.7%), 40.9% of which were grade 3 or higher. No statistically significant differences were found in the two cohorts (p > 0.9999), as shown in Table 3.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Here we reported a study focusing on the possible impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy. Overall, 89 patients received CAR T-cell therapy, of whom 37 had a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Comparing the two cohorts of patients (COVID- versus COVID+), patients had significantly poor IPI (48.1% vs. 21.6%, p = 0.0109), higher levels of LDH (44.2% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.0025) and ferritin (21.2% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.0025), prior to CAR T-cell infusion. However, when comparing all other pre-infusion variables as shown in Table 1, as well as post-infusion CAR T-cell toxicity in terms of CRS and ICANS, no significant differences were found.

As seen in the univariate analysis, the difference between the two cohorts in terms of IPI, LDH level and ferritin pre-CAR T-cell infusion was statistically significant. In fact, patients in the COVID- cohort had a higher disease burden before the CAR T-cell infusion, as represented by these variables. This may explain the worse survival in terms of PFS and OS for the COVID- cohort. In particular, mPFS and mOS were not reached in the COVID + cohort compared to 5.47 and 19 months in the COVID- cohort. Hirayama et al. found that low pre-LD LDH levels in B-NHL patients treated with anti-CD19 CAR T-cell were linked to higher CR rates (HR 0.24, p = 0.003) and better PFS (HR 1.37, p = 0.0006). On the contrary, elevated pre-LD LDH indicated higher disease burden and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [22]. The German Lymphoma Alliance confirmed this in 356 patients, showing that high pre-LD LDH and non-response to bridging therapy were associated with worse 12-month PFS (HR 1.443, p = 0.011) and OS (HR 1.439, p = 0.038) [23].

Due to SARS-CoV-2 infection, 2 patients (2.2%) delayed their scheduled leukapheresis by 14 days and 35 days, and 2 patients delayed their scheduled CAR T-cell infusion by 20 days and 65 days from the date of admission for CAR T-cell infusion. Despite these COVID-19-related delays, no statistically significant difference in PFS was observed between the two groups.

In the COVID + cohort, we analyzed the timing of SARS-CoV-2 infections, distinguishing those occurring before or after CAR T-cell infusion. A total of 37 patients experienced 50 SARS-CoV-2 infections, with 2 to 4 events per patient and an overall mortality rate, in the COVID + cohort of 5.4% (2/37 patients). In our series a total of 4 patients died from COVID-19, two of whom were undergoing lymphoma treatment after CAR T-cell therapy. Of these, two deaths occurred in 2020 during the wild-type variant surge, one in 2021 during the Alpha/Delta wave, and one in 2022 when Omicron became dominant. Notably, Omicron showed reduced virulence compared to earlier variants. Among 11 patients infected in 2022, only one died, while the other three deaths happened during the more virulent wild-type, Alpha, and Delta periods. Table 4 compares our findings with published studies on COVID-19 in CAR T-cell patients. The mortality rate in our cohort (5.4%) is notably lower than that reported by the EPICOVIDEHA registry (31.2% overall mortality in oncohematology patients in 2020, rising to 47.6% in those treated with CAR-T cells as the last line of therapy) [24], as well as in the pre-vaccination studies by Spanjaart et al. (41.1%) [17] and Busca et al. (33%) [16]. In the vaccinated cohort analyzed by Van Doesum et al. [25], mortality dropped from 43.5% in 2020 to 13% in 2022, with an overall rate of 31.2%. This decline is likely attributed to improved access to new antivirals and the combined effect of vaccination and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (NmAb) [25]. Similarly, Cheok et al. [26] reported a lower mortality rate of 14% in vaccinated patients who received early antiviral therapy to prevent severe or critical disease [27].

sec.p: CAR T-cell-induced B-cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia increase the risk of prolonged infection after infusion. The cohorts from Spanjaart et al., Busca et al., Cheok et al., and Van Doesum et al. reported median times from SARS-CoV-2 infection to CAR T-cell infusion of 7.4, 5.6, 9.0, and 6.6 months, respectively [16, 17, 25, 26]. This was consistent with our findings, where only 8 patients developed SARS-CoV-2 infection within 90 days of infusion (7 within 60 days), with no deaths. Within 180 days, 12 patients were infected, with only one death. The median time from CAR T-cell infusion to SARS-CoV-2 was 11.3 months. Although SARS-CoV-2 infection remains a risk for months after CAR T-cell infusion, several factors have contributed to a reduction in severe COVID-19 cases and mortality among CAR-T-treated patients compared to the early pandemic. These include centralized patient management, early antiviral therapy (with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir used in 56.6% of cases in our study), prophylaxis with neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (NmAb), the vaccination campaign, and the emergence of less virulent variants (Omicron from November 2021). Notably, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir did not cause drug interactions in CAR-T patients, unlike other hematologic therapies.

In our series 54 patients (60.7%) received a median of 3 doses (1–5) of one of the available SARS-CoV-2 vaccines before becoming candidates for CAR T-cell therapy. Post CAR T-cell infusion, 30.3% of patients were vaccinated, with a median of 2 doses (1–4). An EPICOVIDEHA study evaluated vaccination and NmAb therapy (sotrovimab, casirivimab-imdevimab, bamlanivimab-etesevimab) in CAR T-cell patients with COVID-19 (2020–July 2022) [25]. Vaccinated patients (40.6% with ≥ 1 dose) had longer intervals from CAR-T infusion to COVID-19 (386 vs. 159 days), milder disease, shorter hospital stays (7 vs. 27.5 days), and fewer ICU admissions (p = 0.054). Mortality decreased from 33.3 to 14.2%, though not significant. Omicron infections were less severe, with fewer ICU admissions, despite similar hospital stays. Van Doesum et al. stressed the need for ≥ 3 vaccine doses for effective protection, as 73% received only 1–2 doses. Fourth-dose recipients in EPICOVIDEHA had lower mortality (3.9%), and none of six patients with three or four doses in Van Doesum’s cohort died [25]. Two pre-vaccine CAR-T studies reported ICU admissions of 39.3% and 43.3% and COVID-19 mortality rates of 41.1% and 33% [16, 17], linked to immunodepression, prior therapies, and active disease. The approval of mRNA vaccines (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273), antivirals (remdesivir, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir), and monoclonal antibodies (casirivimab-imdevimab, sotrovimab) reduced mortality. The EPICOVIDEHA registry showed that in vaccinated oncohematology patients (91% with ≥ 2 doses), 30-day mortality dropped from 22 to 9% [28]. Cheok et al. compared 65 vaccinated CAR-T patients (who had COVID-19 between 2021 and 2022) with 29 unvaccinated patients (who had COVID-19 between 2020–2021)26,27. Early antiviral therapy from the UK Covid Medicine Delivery Unit (CDMU) cut severe COVID-19 risk by 90% and reduced mortality from 63.2 to 13.9%. Despite progress, mortality in vaccinated CAR-T patients was 14%, highlighting the need for continued advancements in vaccines and treatments.

Additionally, in our study 21 patients (23.6%) received prophylactic tixagevimab-cilgavimab, with 4 patients (19%) receiving it before infusion and 17 patients (81%) after infusion. As shown in the EPICOVIDEHA study by Marchesi et al. [29], tixagevimab-cilgavimab prophylaxis did not significantly reduce COVID-19 severity or mortality but was associated with fewer hospitalizations and shorter stays in breakthrough cases. Patients with prophylaxis were more likely to be untreated or receive corticosteroids, while controls more often received antivirals. The combined effect of vaccines and prophylaxis likely helps prevent progression to severe COVID-19.

Our study has some limitations, primarily its retrospective design, and the fact that it was conducted during a period of constant evolution in the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in terms of emerging variants and advancements in therapeutic management, including new vaccines and antiviral treatments. To overcome the aforementioned two potential confounding factors (type of vaccines and variants of infections), we had initially considered the case-case time control design. In fact, there are situations in which the temporal trend of exposure in cases and controls are very different. This is especially the case when the outcome in study is death (our primary endpoint). If so, the time trend could in turn be affected by confounding from indication. In these situations, the adjustment for the time trend introduces a new distortion that can even be stronger than that produced without adjusting for the trend.

Thus, we have decided to report the exact and real picture of what happened. To note, even if not statistically significant, the median follow-up of COVID + patients were higher than the one of COVID- ones. Deaths due to COVID or due to COVID-related causes - net of the censorship declared in the methods at the time of the start of a subsequent therapy – are only 2.

Thus, as confirmed by univariate and multivariate analyses the differences in OS and in PFS derived only by the 3 worse characteristics on the COVID- cohort at baseline. These characteristics are not associated with COVID infections. To sum up, what could be considered bias in our analyses actually support our hypothesis, namely that COVID per se did not affect the prognosis of patients. Despite these limitations, we found that early treatment of patients undergoing CAR T-cell did not negatively impact survival in patients with COVID-19, especially for infections occurring after 2022. Among the 89 LBCL patients treated with CAR T-cells, we observed 28 deaths (31.5%): 4 in the COVID + cohort (2 due to PD and 2 due to COVID-19) and 24 in the COVID- cohort (18 from PD, 2 from grade 5 ICANS, 2 from COVID-19 during post CAR T-cell lymphoma therapy, 1 from septic shock, and 1 from myocardial infarction). These findings suggest that patients in the COVID- cohort had more aggressive disease, resulting in higher mortality from disease progression. Only 2 patients died from SARS-CoV-2 infection, in the COVID + cohort, indicating that COVID-19 is not associated with outcomes in the CAR T settings, also in terms of toxicities. Given the retrospective nature of the study and ongoing advancements in COVID-19 treatment and viral evolution, a robust association cannot be stated, highlighting the need for larger studies to draw more conclusive results.

In conclusion, we found no difference in survival among CAR T-cell recipients with COVID-19, which is notably better than previously reported. This improvement is likely due to the progressive implementation of vaccination programs, prophylaxis, early antiviral therapies, and the emergence of less virulent SARS-CoV-2 variants, all contributing to reduced severity and mortality of COVID-19 in these patients. These data are reassuring for the clinical management of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the context of cellular therapies, which remains highly relevant today as the virus continues to circulate—particularly among onco-hematological patients—showing that in our series survival was not significantly impacted by the infection.
